title: No silicon wafer: memory built inside glass-core package substrates
idea: Forced limit: no memory die. Substrate makers deposit oxide-TFT gain-cell tiers directly on the glass core of advanced package substrates (about 510x515 mm panels), so the substrate under the processor is itself a near-memory tier.
why: Supply and data movement: package-substrate makers become memory makers, and the wire to the processor is millimetres long, cutting I/O energy toward 1 pJ/bit.

title: Composite: new-die cache fronts reclaimed DDR4 dies on CXL modules
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: a CXL module pairs one new DDR5 die as a write-back cache with seven reclaimed DDR4 dies, run by an existing controller re-spun with one changed metal mask to add the caching and wear map.
why: Supply: converts recycled dies into near-new performance capacity, cutting fresh-bit demand ~85% per module.

title: Triple-vote modules built from reject dies, cubesat-style
idea: Cubesat builders fly three COTS memories with majority voting instead of rad-hard parts. A 10-person shop builds modules where three near-free reject-grade dies hold each word and a small FPGA votes bitwise and scrubs, giving industrial-grade reliability from scrap.
why: Turns zero-value fallout into high-reliability supply: 3x silicon at ~0.1x die cost.

title: Magnify DIMM lifespan 3x via a reclamation exchange
idea: Hyperscalers retire servers every 4-6 years with healthy DIMMs; robotic test-and-rebin centers grade them (retention, row-hammer threshold, speed) and repackage them into CXL Type-3 memory-expander sleds resold as a capacity tier with a 3-year warranty.
why: Supply without a fab: ~10-15% of annual server DRAM demand could be served by reused modules at ~20-30% of new price.

title: Aquaporin membranes turn brackish groundwater into fab ultrapure water
idea: Aquaporin channels pass water near the diffusion limit while rejecting ions. Membranes with embedded biomimetic aquaporins treat brackish aquifers in the U.S. Southwest into UPW feed at lower pressure, and close the loop on fab wastewater.
why: Opens water-scarce sites and cuts water-treatment energy ~20-30%, removing a siting barrier for new U.S. fabs.

title: Cast-mono solar silicon substrates for error-tolerant DRAM wafers
idea: Inverts 'DRAM needs prime CZ wafers from high-purity quartz crucibles': use cast-mono silicon from the solar industry, polished and given gettering layers; the extra leakage-tail cells from metals and dislocations fall within the 1% cell budget.
why: Scarce resource: sidesteps the Spruce Pine crucible chokepoint and could halve substrate cost; the risk is dislocations killing transistors in clusters.

title: Ship periphery to logic fabs: array-only DRAM wafers bonded to CMOS
idea: Rearrange array and periphery: the DRAM fab builds only cell arrays, and a mature-node logic foundry builds the sense amps, decoders and I/O on a separate wafer. The two are hybrid-bonded wafer to wafer, as Xtacking does for NAND.
why: Fact 7: periphery is ~49% of the die. Moving it out nearly doubles the bits each DRAM-fab wafer yields and draws on abundant logic capacity.

title: Periodic action: staggered counter-cyclical capex rotation under antitrust safe harbor
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace synchronized boom-bust fab building with a published rotation where each maker adds capacity in assigned years, supervised under a government safe harbor and backed by offtake guarantees in its slot.
why: Pig-cycle volatility: smooths supply so 4x price spikes and loss years are both dampened.

title: No silicon: roll-to-roll MoS2 memory grown on copper foil
idea: Forced limit: the channel and substrate must be non-Si. Monolayer MoS2 is grown by CVD on a continuous copper foil web, transferred to glass or polyimide, and patterned into gain-cell access transistors whose wide bandgap gives sub-fA leakage.
why: Lower leakage reduces refresh, and 2D channels allow scaling without a wafer; supply comes from the copper-foil battery industry.

title: Staktek-Style Package Stacking to Bypass the TSV Bottleneck
idea: Revive the 1990s Staktek/Dense-Pac technique of stacking finished, fully tested packages with flex-frame rails: towers of 4-8 conventional wire-bonded DDR5 packages per site build 256-512 GB capacity RDIMMs on ordinary OSAT lines instead of TSV lines.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV stacks use ~3x the wafer area per bit and lose 20-30% yield; package stacking uses standard dies, known-good packages and idle OSAT capacity for the capacity tier, freeing TSV capacity for HBM.

title: Gridded one-direction layouts for every DRAM layer
idea: Po: the chip only has straight lines. Array and periphery are redesigned so every critical layer is unidirectional lines on a fixed pitch made by self-aligned quadruple patterning, with shapes defined only by DUV cut masks; a gridded 1D periphery cell library replaces 2D shapes.
why: 1D patterns print reliably at ~18-20 nm half pitch with ArF immersion, recovering most of EUV's density; mask count rises modestly while ~$150-380M per avoided EUV scanner is saved; attacks capital and single-supplier risk.

title: Ballroom-free fab: wafers travel only through sealed nitrogen tubes
idea: Particles kill yield only at the wafer surface, so cleanliness need exist only in the few liters around the wafer, not in a 10,000 m^2 class-1 ballroom. Connect tools with sealed N2-purged wafer conveyor tubes and FOUP-docked load ports so the building needs only gray-space HVAC.
why: Capital and energy: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and >40% of fab energy; removing the ballroom cuts both sharply.

title: Irvine Sensors cubes: edge-wired DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors stacked bare memory dies into edge-wired cubes for military use in the 1990s, and the method never went mainstream. Fix: laminate 8-16 thinned standard DDR dies, route their pads to the cube's side face, and pattern the side wiring with 1990s thick-film lithography, giving high-capacity stacks for CXL and server modules without TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax: capacity (not bandwidth) stacks avoid TSV area (~3x wafer area per bit) and its 20-30% yield loss, leaving HBM-grade wafers for AI.

title: Lease bits not chips: vendor-owned memory with cascade redeployment
idea: Inverts 'the buyer owns the DRAM': vendors keep title and rent capacity per GB-month, then pull returned modules down a cascade (AI training -> inference -> enterprise -> edge -> consumer), re-binning at each step.
why: Each die serves 2-3 lifetimes instead of one, raising usable supply ~1.5-2x over a decade from the same wafers and smoothing the vendor revenue cycle that drives under-investment.

title: Blessing in disguise: failed HBM stacks rebinned as HBM-lite via TSV bypass
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: build redundant TSV bypass lanes in every core die so a 12-high stack with one or two dead layers is re-addressed and sold as an 8-high 'HBM-lite' instead of scrap.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: converts much of that loss into sellable capacity.

title: Ga: Abundance-screened bill-of-materials procurement rule for memory
idea: Learning from China's 2023 gallium and germanium export controls, a federal procurement rule scores memory by mass-weighted element supply concentration and gives price preference to non-volatile memories built only from abundant elements.
why: Steers demand and venture money toward chokepoint-free non-volatile memory, cutting systemic supply risk.

title: Eliminate the boom-bust cycle: allied strategic DRAM reserve
idea: Eliminate the price cycle that suppresses investment: a US/allied agency buys packaged DRAM and wafers in gluts, stores them in dry nitrogen, and releases them inside a price band in shortages, like a petroleum reserve.
why: A 2-3 month reserve would blunt 4x price spikes and let makers commit capex counter-cyclically.

title: No private stockpiles: Strategic DRAM Reserve buying known-good die
idea: Self-imposed limit: only the state may hoard. A federal reserve buys wafers and known-good dies during price troughs, stores them under nitrogen, and releases them in spikes under a price-trigger rule, as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve does.
why: Damps the 4x price swings and gives makers a buyer of last resort in downturns, which supports steady capex.

title: Shipyard block construction: arrays at memory fabs, periphery at logic foundries
idea: Shipyards build hull blocks in parallel at different yards and join them. Make array-only DRAM wafers at memory fabs, and periphery/IO/control wafers at underused U.S. logic foundries on 28-16 nm. Join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, as CMOS-bonded-array NAND does.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die: array wafers carry ~1.7-1.9x more bits. Periphery moves onto U.S. logic capacity, raising bits per DRAM wafer with no new memory fab.

title: Nanoimprint-only DRAM capacitor and bitline patterning consortium
idea: Box[Fab=nanoimprint lithography for repetitive array layers x Owner=multi-maker consortium sharing master templates x Finance=template cost pooling]: pattern the highly periodic capacitor-hole and bitline layers by NIL instead of EUV, with a consortium sharing the master-template and defect-learning cost.
why: Capital intensity: cuts 2-4 EUV layers per wafer and ~30-40% of litho capex for array layers.

title: Retention-fingerprint registry that authenticates resold DRAM chips
idea: Copying sneaker-resale authentication, a 10-person service records each chip's random weak-cell retention map, a natural PUF, at first sale. Any later reseller re-reads the map in minutes to prove the chip is genuine and not relabeled.
why: Counterfeits poison grey-market supply; authentication lets secondary DRAM reach defense and enterprise buyers.

title: Pollinator nectar credit: per-bit tax credit for capacitor-free memory
idea: Flowers pay pollinators per visit, not upfront. A production tax credit pays per shipped gigabit of U.S.-made, capacitor-free, DRAM-class memory (<=100 ns, >=1e15 cycles), tapering as volume grows.
why: Rewards output rather than announcements and steers capital to cells that mature fabs can build.

title: Synthetic crucible silica from any beach sand via chloride distillation
idea: Purity is a chemistry problem, not geology: carbochlorinate ordinary sand to SiCl4, fractionally distill to 9N, flame-hydrolyze to fused silica soot, and form crucibles by slip casting plus arc fusion. Inputs are only Si, O, C, Cl and H.
why: Scarce resource: breaks Spruce Pine's >80% hold on HPQ crucibles, and fully synthetic walls lower metal contamination in ingots.

title: Unbundled HBM: independent U.S. stacker buys dies, builds stacks
idea: Rearrange the HBM value chain: DRAM makers sell known-good core dies, and a U.S. OSAT does TSV reveal, hybrid bonding and stack test. The stacks pair with a foundry-made base die from any customer, as in the logic chiplet market.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): a specialist stacker can raise stack yield and creates onshore HBM output with no DRAM front end. Supply widens beyond the three integrated vendors.

title: CXL reclaim cards: retired DDR4 RDIMMs fused onto CXL expanders
idea: Combine the hyperscale server-decommissioning stream with a CXL Type-3 controller card that hosts 8-16 retired DDR4 RDIMMs, after an at-speed retest, as a pooled far-memory tier behind DDR5 hosts. Firmware remaps weak rows, and patrol-scrub data sets each card's refresh rate.
why: Gives 3-5 more years of service to exabytes of DDR4 that would otherwise be shredded. Adds roughly 10-20% usable fleet capacity at about 1/4 the $/GB of new DDR5, with no wafer starts.

title: National EUV scanner-hour utility shared by memory startups
idea: Time-slicing a $200M asset: a national center owns EUV scanners and sells exposure hours. Startups' DRAM wafers travel in sealed FOUPs by courier, get their 5-7 EUV layers, and return to the startups' smaller DUV-only fabs.
why: Removes the single largest capex item from entrants and keeps scanners near 100% utilized. Entrant fab capex falls ~40%.

title: Mercury Delay Line Reborn as a Fiber Loop Broadcasting Weights
idea: Revive EDSAC's 1949 mercury delay line as a recirculating optical-fiber loop: a model's weights circulate as WDM pulses in a ~100 km fiber spool (100 wavelengths at 400 Gb/s hold ~2.5 GB, one lap every 0.5 ms) with an amplifier-regenerator, and dozens of accelerators tap the loop through passive splitters, each reading every weight once per lap, matching per-token decode cadence.
why: Replaces N per-accelerator DRAM weight copies with one in-flight copy and amortizes each weight access over N readers: ~10-50x lower energy per access at N>=32; built from telecom optics supply chains, not DRAM fabs.

title: Block copolymer self-assembly prints hexagonal capacitor arrays
idea: Po: chips are grown, not made. A cylinder-forming high-chi block copolymer self-assembles into a hexagonal lattice matching the DRAM capacitor honeycomb; a coarse ArF guide pattern at 3x pitch registers it (density multiplication), and the cylinders become the hard mask for storage-node holes.
why: Defines the densest DRAM layer without EUV or quadruple patterning, saving ~3-4 litho/etch passes; attacks litho capital.

title: Camel-mode chiller-free data centers enabled by 125 C memory
idea: Like camels that let body temperature rise rather than sweat away water, specify memory and modules qualified for 10 years at 125 C junction so halls can be air-cooled with 50 C intake in deserts with no evaporative towers; temperature-aware refresh keeps data intact.
why: Opens cheap-power, water-scarce sites (e.g., Arizona, Gulf) without water permits and removes 20-40% of cooling energy, making new AI capacity and its memory deployable faster.

title: Kalundborg industrial symbiosis around a U.S. memory fab
idea: Adapted from Denmark's Kalundborg park, where plants trade waste streams: co-locate a U.S. fab with an onsite air-separation unit (nitrogen, argon, neon), a sulfuric-acid regenerator, a greenhouse and a data center that buys both fab output and its low-grade heat.
why: Cuts purchased chemicals and gases ~20-30%, plus water and logistics exposure, making domestic fab operating cost competitive with Asia (scarce resources, energy, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Containerized hybrid-bond stacking micro-OSATs at data centers
idea: Box[Fab=back-end only x Scale=shipping-container cleanrooms x Integration=custom-height stacks on demand x Owner=data-center operator]: KGD wafers ship to modular back-end pods beside AI campuses that hybrid-bond, test and package memory stacks to each cluster's needs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: back-end capacity in months, not years; removes Asian OSAT bottleneck for stacking.

title: Kalundborg symbiosis park: fab, data center and grid trade byproducts
idea: Kalundborg's industrial park trades steam, gypsum and water between plants. Co-site a DRAM fab with a hyperscale data center and a power plant. Reclaimed fab water cools the data center, data-center heat drives fab HVAC reheat and UPW preheat, spent acids go to fertilizer, and known-good dies cross the fence straight into servers.
why: Energy and water: cuts fab water ~40% and energy ~15%, opening arid U.S. sites and removing logistics and packaging duplication.

title: No silicon wafer: multi-project panel shuttles for memory startups
idea: Forced limit: startups cannot afford a wafer lot. A panel foundry runs shared Gen 6 glass shuttles where 100 or more startups each get a tile of oxide-memory process, at about 1/100 of a mask set and lot.
why: Capital: cuts prototype cost from millions to tens of thousands of dollars and speeds non-Si memory innovation.

title: Substitute ownership with leased bits that cascade down tiers
idea: Swap buying DRAM for Memory-as-a-Service: the memory maker keeps title to every module, leases it to cloud first, then recalls and re-leases it to enterprise, edge and consumer tiers, with RFID/serial telemetry tracking wear and retention.
why: Each bit serves 2-3 lifetimes instead of 1, multiplying effective supply per wafer by ~1.5-2x and turning capex into an annuity that smooths the price cycle.

title: Page-age compression ladder across ns-to-hour timescales
idea: Time-scale tiering: hardware in the CXL expander compresses pages by idle age. Pages idle for 1 s get LZ4, 1 min gets zstd with dictionary, and 1 h gets deduplicated, compressed and parked in flash, while hot pages stay raw.
why: Most of a fleet's DRAM holds data idle for seconds or more. The ladder lifts effective capacity 1.6-2.5x, a supply gain that is purely logic.

title: Synthetic-rubber program: government-owned, contractor-operated memory plants
idea: In 1942-44 the U.S. built 51 synthetic-rubber plants in about two years as government-owned, contractor-operated (GOCO) sites with pooled process licenses. Do the same for DRAM: government-owned shells and tools, operators who bid to run them under pooled-IP agreements, and privatization after a decade.
why: U.S. manufacturability: removes private capital risk for moving from 1-2% to 10%+ U.S. share, and pooled licenses allow a fast build cadence.

title: Nesting: fab-in-fab DRAM lines inside idle logic, solar and LED shells
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: insert a compact 10-20k wspm DRAM module line into existing idle cleanroom bays (shuttered 300 mm logic, solar-cell, LED or MEMS fabs) reusing their utilities, gas yards and permits.
why: Capital and time: cuts greenfield cost ~30-40% and time-to-wafer by ~2 years; boosts U.S. manufacturability.

title: Eliminate laptop-memory dead end: SO-DIMM-to-CXL carrier card
idea: Eliminate the form-factor dead end of laptop memory: an FPGA-based CXL Type-3 card hosts eight mixed DDR4 SO-DIMMs harvested from e-waste laptops and presents them to modern servers as a slow capacity tier; $1M covers board design, controller IP and a 200-card pilot.
why: Turns e-waste SO-DIMMs into server far-memory at a fraction of new DDR5 cost.

title: Polyglot CXL card that accepts any mix of harvested DRAM chips
idea: Extreme user: GPU-mining and phone e-waste full of orphaned DDR3, DDR4, LPDDR4 and GDDR5 chips. A 10-person team designs an FPGA-based CXL Type-3 card with swappable daughterboards and per-channel PHY profiles, so any tested mix of harvested chips becomes one pooled memory device; boards go through contract SMT, and the team owns firmware and test.
why: Opens a stream of orphan chip types that no module standard can absorb, at perhaps $1-2/GB effective.

title: Biosimilar interchangeability: fast-track qualification for U.S.-made DRAM
idea: Adapted from the FDA biosimilar pathway: a NIST-run reference test suite and shared reliability datasets let a new U.S. maker earn an 'interchangeable' designation proving JEDEC equivalence, which OEMs accept in place of 12-18 months of bespoke qualification.
why: Qualification delay is a hidden entry barrier; cutting it to ~4-6 months gets U.S. bits to market about a year sooner (U.S. manufacturability, supply).

title: Zn: Indium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cells built in idle LCD fabs
idea: Retool depreciated Gen-6/8 display lines to make ZTO (Zn, Sn, O only; no In or Ga) 2T0C gain-cell DRAM on glass at ~1 um rules, stacking a few layers; one Gen-8 panel yields ~100 GB per layer, diced into CXL capacity-tier tiles.
why: Glass panel area is ~100x cheaper per m2 than 300 mm wafer area and needs no EUV; avoids In/Ga chokepoints; a capacity tier at a few $/GB.

title: Magnify usable capacity: compression engines in every CXL controller
idea: Put line-rate LZ4/zstd-class compression engines in CXL memory controllers, back them with an OCP procurement spec and OS policy (compressed tiers on by default), and expose compressed capacity as plain addressable memory.
why: Server memory typically compresses 2-3x; effective usable supply grows ~1.5-2x on warm pages without a single new wafer.

title: Wine second-label program for partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Adapted from chateaux selling declassified barrels under a second label: dies with one or two dead bank groups are fused off and sold as lower-density SKUs (e.g., 24 Gb from 32 Gb) under a separate brand. Controllers and firmware are told the remapped topology.
why: Turns part of early-ramp yield loss (often 5-15%) into salable bits; adds ~3-8% bits per wafer during node ramps (cost per bit).

title: Depreciated legacy DRAM lines kept running as a regulated utility
idea: Inverts 'old nodes are scrapped or converted when the next node arrives': a public-private utility buys fully depreciated 1x/2x-nm DRAM lines that vendors plan to convert to HBM and runs them at cash cost for consumer, automotive and industrial DRAM.
why: Capital: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so a depreciated line's cost per bit can rival a new node; keeps capacity online instead of losing it to HBM conversion.

title: Corolla node: freeze one DRAM process for ten years
idea: Ideal: a node whose tools cost nothing. Closest achievable: run a 1y/1z-nm DDR5 process unchanged for a decade on fully depreciated tools and grow volume by moving tool sets from fabs that upgrade, instead of chasing each new node.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4): cost per bit falls ~40% once tools are paid off, beating the 10-20% a node shrink buys.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as capacitor hole templates
idea: Po: aluminum drills the holes. A deposited aluminum film is two-step anodized so self-ordering yields hexagonal nanopores at 40-60 nm pitch with aspect ratios over 100:1; pore registry is seeded by a DUV-patterned pre-texture, and the alumina template is lined TiN/high-k/TiN to form storage capacitors.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (needs AR ~115) while removing EUV and the hardest high-aspect-ratio etch, using room-temperature electrochemistry; attacks capital and density.

title: Cash-settled DRAM bit futures damp the cobweb shortage cycle
idea: The DRAM boom-bust behaves like a delay-line oscillator: a 3-5 year capacity lag chasing a ~1-year demand signal (cobweb model). A cash-settled Gb futures curve out to 4 years gives fabs a forward price to hedge expansions and buyers a way to lock supply, effectively shortening the control loop's delay.
why: Supply stability: lowers the peak-to-trough amplitude that produced the 4x price spike, and hedged revenue reduces risk premia on new capacity.

title: AerCap for fab tools: a lessor that redeploys scanners between fabs
idea: Aircraft lessors own planes and re-lease them across airlines. A capitalized lessor owns ArF scanners and deposition/etch fleets with standardized install kits, leases them on 3-5 year terms, and moves them when a fab downsizes. Asset-backed securities secured by the tools fund the fleet.
why: Capital intensity (~55% of wafer cost is depreciation): entrants avoid upfront tool capex, and industry-wide tool utilization rises out of cyclical idling.

title: 28 nm inline compression buffer that doubles bits per DIMM
idea: Ideal: every bit holds two. Closest achievable at trailing nodes: a 28 nm buffer chip that replaces the RCD/data buffer runs line-rate base-delta and LZ compression with a metadata cache, presenting 1.5-2x logical capacity; KV-cache, zero pages and sparse tensors compress well.
why: Usable capacity +40-100% depending on data, with no new memory wafers.

title: Telemetry-backed warranties that make used DRAM bankable
idea: Ideal: used memory is trusted as much as new. Closest achievable with no new fab: an insurer underwrites 3-year warranties on second-life DIMMs, priced from each module's logged correctable-error history and burn-in screen, so clouds accept refurbished DRAM in production.
why: Reuse demand unlock: lets 20-30% of retired server DRAM re-enter service.

title: Substitute silicon DRAM in edge devices with roll-to-roll foil memory
idea: Swap silicon DRAM in IoT, wearables and appliance controllers for oxide gain-cell memory made on polyimide foil by roll-to-roll sputter/ALD lines at <=300 C, freeing silicon bits for servers.
why: Moves the low-density, high-unit-count share of demand off DRAM wafers; R2R capex per m^2 is ~100x lower than a fab.

title: Eliminate test hardware: bootable signed DIMM health certificate
idea: Eliminate expensive ATE for used-memory trust: a free bootable image runs 8-hour retention, pattern and row-hammer tests on any host and signs the result with the module's SPD serial; ~$600k builds the software, signing service and three pilot broker integrations in 18 months.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in reuse; certified used DRAM sells at 40-60% of new and unlocks stranded DDR4 inventory.

title: UCIe memory die bank: interchangeable known-good DRAM chiplets
idea: Fuse a standard die-to-die interface (UCIe/BoW) with a commodity exchange. Any qualified small maker sells known-good DRAM chiplets with a common footprint, pinout and test spec through a brokerage that warrants interchangeability, the way a grain elevator does.
why: Lowers entry barriers for new memory makers (no package or brand ecosystem needed) and diversifies supply beyond three firms.

title: Tunneling-clock deposit-refund system pays owners to return memory
idea: Each module carries a floating-gate cell whose tunneling charge loss acts as a powerless chronometer. A deposit charged at sale is refunded on return, scaled by measured age and wear, which funds take-back and guarantees recyclers a supply stream.
why: Non-hyperscaler server memory take-back is low; a deposit-refund like bottle bills could lift returns above 80%.

title: Capacity frozen: retrofit CXL compression expanders for cold pages
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new DRAM bits at all. A drop-in CXL card with line-rate LZ/ZSTD-class hardware compresses cold pages, so each physical GB serves 2-3 logical GB with hot pages left uncompressed.
why: Do the job with less: 1.5-2.5x effective capacity on the memory-bound tier.

title: DIMM deposit-refund system modeled on bottle bills
idea: Fuse beverage-container deposit laws with memory. A $2-5 per-module deposit is added at sale and refunded when the module comes back through certified collectors, who feed the reuse and re-binning chain instead of shredders.
why: Raises module recovery from under 20% to 80%+ (bottle bills hit about 90%), building a reliable feedstock for second-life memory supply.

title: $1B 3D-DRAM prize judged on a public test vehicle
idea: Ideal: infinite inventors working for free. Closest achievable: a Longitude-style prize paid for the first 3D DRAM stack hitting 26+ tiers, 64 ms retention and 1e15 cycles on an open test vehicle, with winning IP licensed into a common pool.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): prizes typically draw 10-20x their value in private R&D.

title: Quorum-sensing escrow that auto-triggers fab expansion at threshold
idea: Bacteria act together only when signal-molecule concentration crosses a threshold. Buyers deposit refundable commitments into an escrow; when committed volume for a fab phase crosses the preset level, the funds release as prepayment and construction starts automatically.
why: Turns fragmented demand into bankable capex and removes years of deliberation from capacity response.

title: Minify writes to one: model weights in stamped ROM cartridges
idea: Inference weights, the bulk of AI memory, are written once per model; store them in 100+ layer 3D via-programmed ROM nanoimprint-stamped from a master, with DRAM-class random read, shipped as swappable per-model cartridges so DRAM holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Stamped ROM has no write circuitry, capacitor or refresh, reaching NAND-like ~$0.05-0.1/GB (~100x below DRAM); endurance is unlimited for reads by architecture.

title: Open DRAM PDK: royalty-free cell, periphery and process recipes
idea: Reverse IP from secret to open: a federally funded consortium publishes a full 1x-nm-class DRAM process recipe, cell and sense-amp library and test programs under a royalty-free license, backed by a defensive patent pool. New fabs then license nothing from incumbents.
why: Lowers the entry barrier of years of process learning and litigation risk. Time from start to first good wafer for a new U.S. entrant could fall from ~5 years to ~2.

title: Substitute new dies with remanufactured dies from retired server DIMMs
idea: Swap virgin DRAM for remanufactured DRAM: robotic de-soldering lines pull dies off decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs, re-ball them, run retention/row-hammer/BIST screens and re-mount them on new PCBs sold in warranty tiers.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers; hyperscalers retire ~tens of EB of DDR4/DDR5 yearly, and recovering even 20% adds several % of annual bit supply at ~30-50% of new cost per bit.

title: Eliminate retention-fail scrap: sell weak dies as fast-refresh grade
idea: Eliminate the 64 ms retention gate: dies that fail 64 ms but pass 16-32 ms are bought, binned and sold with an SPD flag that forces the controller's existing 2x/4x refresh mode; ~$400k for binning and qualification.
why: Converts retention-tail rejects into usable bits for bandwidth-insensitive capacity tiers at a small refresh-energy penalty.

title: Hyperscaler joint venture owns a cost-plus DRAM fab, Airbus-style
idea: Inverts 'buyers and makers of DRAM are adversaries over margin': 4-6 large buyers form a joint-venture entity that owns a U.S. fab running a licensed process from a second-tier vendor, sells at cost, and splits output pro rata to equity.
why: Cost per bit: strips the 40-60% peak-cycle vendor margin and guarantees offtake that de-risks $15B capex; also adds a U.S. source.

title: Repurpose idle LCD panel fabs for glass-substrate oxide gain cells
idea: Adapted from display makers' Gen-8.5 lines that already deposit IGZO TFTs: retool them to print 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass panels. Thinned CMOS periphery chiplets are bonded onto the panel afterward.
why: Panel lines are cheap per m2 and underused after LCD oversupply; ~10-20x the area of a 300 mm wafer could cut cost per bit for a bulk CXL capacity tier, provided ~0.5-1 um features meet speed targets (cost per bit, capital intensity).

title: Hyperscaler take-or-pay SPVs that own DRAM fab lines
idea: Po: the customer owns the fab. Like LNG trains financed by 20-year take-or-pay contracts, 3-5 hyperscalers fund a special-purpose vehicle that owns a DRAM line run by an incumbent or new entrant, receiving output at cost-plus in proportion to equity.
why: Contracted offtake lets fab debt be priced like infrastructure (~5-6%) instead of chip equity (~12-15%); with depreciation ~55% of wafer cost, a lower WACC cuts cost per bit ~15-25%; attacks capital intensity.

title: Mid-size OEM memory cooperative owning a shared DRAM line
idea: Ideal: memory always available at cost. Closest achievable: auto, industrial, PC and console OEMs jointly fund a line as a cooperative (Airbus-GIE or farm-co-op style) and get allocation in proportion to equity at cost-plus during shortages.
why: Supply security for segments that AI demand crowds out, plus price neutrality.

title: Multi-beam e-beam direct write for cut and contact layers
idea: Po: a million pens instead of one camera. Mask-writer-class multi-beam e-beam columns (~250k beamlets) write only the sparse cut and contact layers directly on wafers while dense lines come from spacer patterning; no masks are needed, so micro-fabs and fast design spins become economical.
why: Cut/contact layers are the ones that otherwise force EUV; writing them maskless avoids EUV and multi-million-dollar mask sets, with throughput suited to ~5-10k wafers/month micro-fabs; attacks capital and U.S. micro-fab viability.

title: National tool bank leasing recertified 300 mm tools to micro-fabs
idea: Worse: make every new fab wait 18-24 months for new tools. Flip: a public-private bank buys used 300 mm DUV scanners, etchers and ALD tools from closing or upgrading fabs, refurbishes them, and leases them on 5-year terms to memory startups and pilot lines.
why: Cuts startup capex ~60-70% and tool lead time to months.

title: Approximate-memory SKU letting AI data decay without refresh
idea: Worse: insist every bit is perfect for neural nets that tolerate noise. Flip: run unrefreshed DRAM for activations and gradients, where the controller maps sign and exponent bits to the strongest-retention rows (from a per-die retention map) and low mantissa bits to weak rows, accepting ~1e-5 bit errors.
why: Zero refresh power, and weak-retention dies become usable, with accuracy loss <0.1% in tolerant models.

title: Eliminate price opacity: public DRAM contract index and cash-settled swaps
idea: Eliminate opaque bilateral pricing: a ~$700k startup gathers anonymized contract and spot trades from buyers, publishes a daily DRAM bit index, and partners with a commodity broker to offer cash-settled swaps.
why: Hedging lets OEMs lock costs and producers fund capacity against a forward curve, damping the cycle.

title: Dual DDR4/DDR5 PHY server CPUs to keep DDR4 in service
idea: Box[Source=installed DDR4 fleet x Integration=CPU memory controller supporting both standards on separate boards x Owner=CPU vendor + hyperscaler]: ship next-gen server CPUs with a combo PHY (as consumer chips did) so retired-platform DDR4 RDIMMs move into new servers unchanged.
why: Extends ~100% of DDR4 fleet life by a server generation; cuts new-DIMM demand without changing either interface.

title: Na: Sodium-ion rack batteries make DRAM durable, deleting database replicas
idea: Rack-level Na-ion batteries hold servers up long enough to flush DRAM to NVMe on power loss, certified as durable, so in-memory databases and caches drop one of their 2-3 durability replicas.
why: Saves 33-50% of DRAM in replicated in-memory clusters; Na-ion avoids Li and Co.

title: Tungsten urban mining from spent sputter targets and chamber shields
idea: Worse: buy fresh Chinese tungsten for every wordline and contact. Flip: collect spent W targets, CVD chamber kits and WF6 scrubber residues across U.S. fabs and refine them electrochemically back to WF6 feedstock in a shared regional plant.
why: Spent targets keep ~70% of their tungsten; a closed loop could cover a large share of fab demand and cut China dependence.

title: No HBM stack scrapped: base-die remap into lower-capacity SKUs
idea: Self-imposed limit: zero stack scrap. Stacks with one or two dead core dies are remapped by base-die logic into 6- or 10-high equivalent SKUs, with channels re-striped, and sold to inference customers who need bandwidth more than capacity.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%; salvaging half of the failed stacks recovers 10-15% of HBM output.

title: Convert idle NAND fabs into stacked DRAM-class memory lines
idea: Po: the NAND fab is a DRAM fab. NAND lines already build 200+-layer stacks with zero EUV using high-aspect-ratio etch, staircase contacts and ALD; a stacked-tier DRAM-class cell (horizontal capacitor tiers sharing a vertical bitline) is designed to reuse >80% of that tool set, so NAND overcapacity is converted rather than new fabs built.
why: Conversion costs a fraction of a $15B greenfield and takes ~1-2 years; tier count, not lithography, buys density; attacks capital intensity and EUV dependence.

title: Self-trimming DRAM design multi-sourced across trailing fabs
idea: Ideal: memory that any fab can make. Closest achievable with no new fab: one design with on-die calibration (sense-amp offset trim, adaptive wordline boost, retention-profiled refresh) and wide margins runs from the same GDS at 3-4 mature DRAM and specialty fabs, like 1980s second-sourcing.
why: Supply resilience: multi-sourcing lowers prices at ~10-15% area overhead.

title: Capillary fluidic self-assembly aggregates DRAM dielets from many small fabs
idea: Micro-fabs make tiny 0.5-1 mm2 DRAM dielets; a central assembler suspends them in liquid where shape-matched recesses and capillary forces seat thousands per minute onto a wafer-scale interposer. Misses are tested and refilled, so many small producers feed one memory product.
why: Distributed manufacturing; small dies yield higher and aggregation needs no high-precision pick-and-place.

title: Civil Reserve Air Fleet adapted: retainer-paid U.S. reserve fab fleet
idea: Adapted from CRAF, where airlines get peacetime contracts in exchange for lending aircraft in crises: U.S. logic, NAND and foundry fabs are paid retainers to keep a qualified DRAM-compatible module flow (capacitor and buried-wordline recipes, spare tool kits) that they can activate within 90 days of a declared shortage.
why: Creates latent U.S. DRAM capacity without idle fabs and can surge ~5-10% of domestic need (U.S. manufacturability, supply resilience).

title: IEA-style allied memory-sharing treaty with crisis allocation
idea: Ideal: no country is ever short of memory. Closest achievable: the U.S., Japan, Korea, Taiwan and the EU commit to share a set % of output and reserves on a declared shortage, with coordinated reserve draws and export priority rules.
why: Geopolitical chokepoints: stops panic buying that amplifies price spikes.

title: Feedback: field-to-fab telemetry loop relaxes over-conservative test guardbands
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: hyperscalers stream anonymized per-die correctable-error and retention telemetry back to the fab, which uses it to retune sort guardbands per lot and safely pass dies currently rejected by worst-case margins.
why: Yield: ~3-8% more passing dies, with less over-test time.

title: Nonvolatile working memory replaces durability replicas in databases
idea: Worse: keep 2-3 DRAM replicas of every in-memory database purely to survive power loss. Flip: place hot state in a nonvolatile DRAM-class tier (FeRAM or MRAM over CXL) that survives power loss, so replicas exist only for availability.
why: Zero refresh, and in-memory database DRAM drops 30-60% as durability-only copies go away.

title: Chokepoint index printed per gigabit steers procurement off banned elements
idea: Compute each die's mass of every element per Gb, weight it by supply concentration (HHI) and geopolitical risk, and print an elemental chokepoint index on the datasheet. Federal and hyperscaler procurement scores bids on cost x (1 + index), so designs built only from Si, Al, Ti, Zr, Cu, O, N and C win.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: converts invisible supply risk into a price signal, pushing W, Co, Ru, Hf, Ta, In and Ga out within one product cycle.

title: Mail carrier's local post offices: a sense amp every 32 cells
idea: Mail goes out from local post offices, not one central depot. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array so every 32 cells get their own sense amp on a ~0.05 fF micro-bitline, which cuts the charge a cell needs from ~5 fF to ~0.3 fF. The capacitor becomes a shallow planar MIM, the array shrinks to 4F^2, and 6 array decks share one sense wafer.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 vs 6F^2 times 6 decks is ~9-10x/mm^2. Dropping the 60-75:1 pillar etch saves ~20% of wafer cost, which pays for the bonding, and the periphery leaves the array die.

title: Eliminate the quartz crucible: cold-crucible levitation silicon growth
idea: Eliminate the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible: grow large-diameter ingots in water-cooled segmented copper cold crucibles where induction fields push the melt off the wall so silicon touches only its own frozen skull.
why: Removes a >80% single-site chokepoint; lower oxygen content also reduces thermal donors that hurt DRAM retention.

title: Glass-fiber draw tower: thermally drawn nanolayer capacitor fibers
idea: Build a centimeter preform of interleaved conductive and high-k glass/polymer layers, then thermally draw it ~10,000x in a fiber tower so the layers thin to ~10 nm. Chop the fiber and stand the pieces in etched wells as pre-built capacitor cores.
why: Charge wall and capital: the capacitor stack comes from a ~$1M draw tower instead of ALD in deep holes, and 1 km of fiber yields billions of cores. University fiber labs can build it.

title: Inductive-coupling stacked DRAM eliminating SF6 Bosch TSV etch
idea: Fuse thinned-die stacking with ThruChip-style inductive or capacitive near-field links between layers, plus wire-bonded or edge-plated power delivery. That removes the SF6/C4F8 Bosch TSV etch and the TSV keep-out area.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (about 3× area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) and fluorinated deep-Si etch, raising HBM-class bits per wafer.

title: On-site flow-chemistry skids that synthesize ALD precursors at the fab
idea: Scale jump from global chemical plant to bench-scale reactor: modular continuous-flow skids at the fab make Hf, Zr and Ti amide and alkoxide precursors from bulk metal chlorides just in time, so no stockpile is shipped across oceans.
why: Removes import chokepoints on high-k and electrode precursors and cuts precursor cost ~30%. Cuts supply risk for capacitor dielectrics.

title: PJM-style capacity market for DRAM wafer starts
idea: Like electricity capacity auctions that pay generators 3 years ahead to exist, a cleared exchange sells standardized forward contracts for 'Gb delivered in quarter Q+12'; fabs post the auction-cleared revenue as collateral to finance tool orders, and buyers hedge 4x price swings.
why: Attacks capital intensity and the boom-bust cycle that delays fab builds; forward revenue visibility could cut cost of capital by 3-5 points and pull capacity forward 12-18 months.

title: DRAM futures exchange lets new fabs borrow against forward sales
idea: Airlines, extreme fuel users, hedge on exchanges. A cleared DRAM futures contract (per Gb of DDR5-equivalent, quarterly delivery) lets AI clouds and phone OEMs hedge, and lets new entrants pre-sell output and borrow against hedged revenue.
why: Lowers cost of capital for new capacity and damps the boom-bust underinvestment behind 4x price spikes.

title: Optical-fiber flame hydrolysis for synthetic quartz crucible liners
idea: Adapted from flame-hydrolysis/OVD deposition used to make ultra-pure fiber preforms in New York: lay a synthetic fused-silica liner on crucibles made from ordinary U.S. quartz, so only the layer that touches the melt needs ultra-high purity.
why: Cuts dependence on Spruce Pine high-purity quartz, a single hurricane-exposed site, by ~80-90% per crucible and adds a second all-U.S. route for CZ wafer growth (scarce resources).

title: Advance market commitment for EUV-free domestic DRAM
idea: Po: the government buys DRAM that does not exist yet. Like vaccine advance market commitments, the U.S. guarantees to buy a set volume (e.g., 1 EB/year for federal and defense fleets) at a fixed price from any domestic producer whose process uses no EUV, paying only on delivery of qualified parts.
why: Removes demand risk for new entrants and hedges the single EUV supplier, paying only for results; attacks capital risk and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Steel-minimill DRAM: small DUV-only fabs on a frozen node
idea: Copy Nucor's electric-arc minimills, which beat integrated mills by being small, flexible and fed on cheap inputs. Build 5k-wafer/month DRAM fabs frozen on a 1y-class (~17 nm) 6F2 process that uses only ArF-immersion SAQP, with no EUV. Depreciate them over 10+ years and sell into the commodity DDR4/LPDDR4 tiers the leaders abandon.
why: Capital intensity and the EUV chokepoint: ~$2-3B vs $15B+, and the depreciation share collapses on a long-frozen node. This frees leading-edge wafers for HBM.

title: MEMS-fab nano-relay bistable memory on underused 200 mm lines
idea: Worse: leave U.S. MEMS and 200 mm fabs underused. Flip: build bistable nano-electromechanical relays, beams latched by adhesion with electrostatic set and reset, as memory cells that hold state mechanically with zero leakage.
why: Zero refresh and zero standby power, made on existing U.S. tools; contact wear limits endurance.

title: Answering-machine grade: partial-good dies with a standard bad-region descriptor
idea: 1980s answering machines used 'audio RAM': dies with known bad cells. Define a JEDEC-style descriptor, fused on die and mirrored in SPD, that lists failed subarrays so OS allocators (badram-style) and CXL controllers skip them. Fabs then sell 90-99%-good dies as a priced grade instead of scrapping them.
why: Recovers yield-fallout dies (often 5-15% of starts on a new node) as usable bits; better cost per bit from existing fabs.

title: On-die microheaters anneal away aging to restore retention for second life
idea: TiN heater meanders under each bank hold the array at 250-300 C for minutes while powered down, re-passivating interface traps with stored hydrogen and relaxing BTI and hot-carrier damage. Retention and Vt margins are restored before resale.
why: Retention-tail drift is a top retirement cause; healing could double service life per die.

title: Pool idle switch packet-buffer SRAM as rack staging memory
idea: Worse: leave hundreds of MB of SRAM idle in every switch and DPU. Flip: expose spare switch packet buffers and DPU SRAM as RDMA-addressable regions that the network OS manages as a rack-level static pool for hot tables and staging buffers.
why: Zero refresh, and installed SRAM is unlocked with no new silicon; access is ~1 us, so it serves staging rather than main memory.
